title: The Kingdom That Ended at His Birth: Strabo, the Nile, and the Seventeen Books
conventions: BCE atlas years '-0100' mean 100 BC; astronomical year = 1 - Y
positions at 0h UT of the civil date; tropical signs of date
Moon and planets only at day precision

birth.stop: Amaseia, born in the valley of the Iris
birth.date_confidence: contested on two counts. The birth year 64/63 BC is a modern chronographic reconstruction, not an ancient datum; Roller (2014) argues for no later than c.60 BC, and Pothecary (1999) holds the traditional date less secure than usually assumed. The two are not reconciled. Birthplace is inference too: Strabo calls Amaseia 'my city' (12.3.39) and 'my fatherland' (12.3.15) but nowhere writes that he was born in it. Month and day default.

stops.stop: Cnossus, Dorylaus is sent for mercenaries
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Strabo dates the episode only by the reign of Mithridates V Euergetes (c.150-120 BC) at Geography 10.4.10; the year here is an ordering device. Note a contradiction inside Strabo himself: 12.3.33 calls Dorylaus the tactician 'my mother's grandfather', while 10.4.10 makes Lagetas the brother of Strabo's maternal grandmother, which would put the tactician a generation further back. Not resolved here.

stops.stop: Rome, an acquaintance with Servilius Isauricus
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, downgraded here from the usual textbook claim. Strabo writes at 12.6.2, in the account of Isaura, only that Publius Servilius surnamed Isauricus was a man 'with whom I was acquainted'. He does not say where, does not mention Rome, and does not mention Caesar. Servilius's death in 44 BC gives a terminus ante quem for the acquaintance and nothing more. The Rome location is the standard modern inference and is flagged as inference. The frequently printed citation 5.3.9 or 5.3.7 for this passage is wrong: Book 5 chapter 3 does not mention him.

stops.segment: Up the Nile with the Prefect
stops.stop: Alexandria, the long residence
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, though a strong one. Extended residence is inferred from the density of firsthand Alexandrian material in Book 17 and is accepted by Roller (2014) and Dueck (2000). Strabo nowhere states how long he stayed. There is no evidence at all that he worked in the Library; that detail is later romance. Coordinates inherited from the canonical Alexandria pin already in use.

stops.stop: Arsinoe on the Red Sea, the fleet he does not sail with
stops.date_confidence: the Arabian expedition is narrated at Geography 16.4.22-24; the staging of the fleet on the Egyptian Red Sea coast is reconstruction. The important point is negative and is attested by silence: Strabo never claims to have gone into Arabia, and his account is built from Gallus and other testimony. The common secondary-literature claim that he was an eyewitness there is wrong.

stops.stop: Amaseia, Typhon under the Burnt Country
stops.date_confidence: attested at Geography 13.4.6 (the Catacecaumene in Lydia) and 16.2.7 (the Orontes in Syria, formerly called Typhon). Place and date of composition unknown; pin is Strabo's own city, date orders the segment. The pairing of these two passages with Cilicia is a common error: neither is Cilician.

stops.stop: Amaseia, Juba is lately dead
stops.date_confidence: attested at Geography 17.3.7, corroborated at 17.3.9, dating the death of Juba II of Mauretania to AD 23/24 and treating it as recent. This is the latest securely datable event in the surviving work and is the argument for a substantially Tiberian final form, against older assumptions of an Augustan edition of c.7 BC. Place of writing unknown; pin is his own city.

stops.stop: Amaseia, and then nothing further
stops.date_confidence: convention, not record. Nothing is attested about Strabo's death: no year, no place, no manner. AD 24 is arithmetic run backward from the Juba notice; retirement to Amaseia is tradition; the pin is his own city because there is nowhere else to put him. No wife, children, tomb, epitaph, ancient biography or contemporary notice survives, and no ancient portrait was ever made.
